title: Refuge, again
hook: taking refuge once more, knowing what it means now
tomorrow: he walked away from two teachers who wanted him. what wasn't enough?

segments.voice: Yesterday, space in the day: the Buddha's eighth thought, a mind with room in it. Room to breathe. Today, an old promise, said again.

Some lines get said so often they wear smooth: a pledge at school, a team chant before a game. Buddhists have one like that, in Pali, three lines, and each line is said three times. Buddham saranam gacchami: I go to the Buddha for refuge. Then the Dhamma, the teaching. Then the Sangha, the community. The three jewels. After years on this path, the old words come back with a sharper question inside them. When you go for refuge, where exactly are you going?
screen: `A PLEDGE, A TEAM CHANT.` → `THREE LINES, THREE TIMES.` → `WHERE EXACTLY ARE YOU GOING?`

segments.voice: The oldest story starts small. Soon after the awakening, two merchants on the road, Tapussa and Bhallika, offer the Buddha rice cakes and honey and ask to be his followers. The Vinaya says they went for refuge to two: the Buddha and the Dhamma. There was no Sangha yet. The third jewel came later, when there were monks to hold it. Now two views, both inside Buddhism. The first says refuge points outward. You lean on a teacher who walked the whole path, a teaching you didn't make up, and friends who catch you when you wobble. A shelter you build alone can't hold you on the day you fall apart. The second view goes to the Buddha's last journey. To grieving Ananda he says: be an island to yourselves, a refuge to yourselves, with the Dhamma as your island. In Chan, the Platform Sutra has Huineng teaching refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha of your own nature. On this view, a jewel outside you that never wakes anything inside you is only a nice word. Neither view throws the other out. People chant the refuges together in one room, and then each one sits alone on a cushion. Three jewels outside, one island inside, and the going is the practice.
screen: `FIRST, ONLY TWO JEWELS.` · `REFUGE POINTS OUTWARD.` · `BE AN ISLAND TO YOURSELVES.` · `TOGETHER, THEN ALONE.` · then, large: `THREE JEWELS.`

segments.voice: If you take refuge, say the three lines out loud, in Pali or English, slowly, once each, and let the sit hold the quiet after. If you don't, say three words softly, Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha, as the names of what Buddhists lean on, and notice which one you'd reach for first.
Refuge: sarana in Pali, a shelter you go to. Three jewels to go to: the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha.
The line to take with you: three jewels, a teacher, a teaching and friends on the road. That's forty-two in this block.

howItsDone: Buddhists go for refuge by reciting the three refuges, usually in Pali and three times over, at the start of temple services, before taking precepts, and in daily chanting at home.

fork.setup: your cousin says taking refuge is outsourcing: 'just trust yourself.' you agree with part of that. what's the best case for the other side?
options: a shelter you build alone can't catch you when you fall; a teacher, teaching and friends can.
there isn't one; the Buddha said trust yourself alone, so your cousin is right.
refuge is only a ceremony, so what it means doesn't really matter.
fork.reveal: both views are Buddhist: be an island to yourselves, and go for refuge to the teacher, the teaching and the community. the best case for refuge outward is that nobody catches themselves alone.

original.note: Pali: refuge, shelter; as in Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge.

chat.meaning: Refuge is turning to the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha; the Buddha also told Ananda to be an island to himself.

tie.story: The first two followers went for refuge to the Buddha and the Dhamma; later the Buddha told Ananda to be an island to himself.

tie.you: who or what do you lean on when you wobble?

Tapussa.meaning: a merchant, one of the first two lay followers

Bhallika.meaning: Tapussa's companion, the other first follower

Sangha.meaning: the community of the Buddha's followers

Huineng.meaning: a Chan master whose teaching the Platform Sutra carries

Vinaya.meaning: the monastic rulebook, with early stories in it

sources.ref: Khuddakapatha 1 (Saranattaya: the three refuges, each said three times)
Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.4 (Tapussa and Bhallika go for refuge to the Buddha and the Dhamma)
Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta) 2.26 (2.33 in Rhys Davids): be an island to yourselves
Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (Huineng on taking refuge in the three jewels of one's own nature)

notes: Mahavagga 1.4: the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika offer rice cakes and honey (mantha and madhupindika) and become the first lay followers with a two-fold refuge (dve-vacika). Confirm 'rice cakes and honey' and 'soon after the awakening'.
DN 16 island passage paraphrased (attadipa, attasarana, dhammadipa). Rhys Davids renders it with 'lamps'; the voice uses 'island', the more common modern reading of dipa. Confirm both are fair.
Platform Sutra: Huineng's teaching of the 'three refuges of one's own nature' paraphrased; no translation quoted. Confirm the Chan framing.
Debate shape: view one (refuge points outward) and view two (island to yourself; refuge in one's own nature) both presented as inside Buddhism, ranked against each other by no one.
Mai's arc: Ông's first night in his new room; Ava (best friend) asks whether the Buddha 'rescues' you.
Surprising fact: the first two lay followers took refuge in only two jewels, because there was no Sangha yet.
